A surviving-fund average can hide the original cohort: keep omitted records in the calculation

Follow eight invented one-year fund records to distinguish a filtered directory average from the complete original cohort, preserve omitted outcomes and test the direction of the gap.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Keep a complete invented cohort beside a filtered end-of-year directory

Interactive planning lab

Mean return across all eight original records-2.00%
Mean return among records still listed8.80%
Listed mean minus complete-cohort mean10.80 pp
Ending value across all eight original positions$78,400

Original, fully observed, invented one-year cohort of eight funds A–H, each with the same opening amount. Base simple total returns, with all income retained and before fees and taxes, are +20%, +12%, +8%, +4%, 0%, −5%, −15% and −40%. All eight complete-period returns and ending values remain known, including for omitted directory records. Omission is an assumed end-of-period listing status, not an estimated closure probability, an actual liquidation or a rule that causes performance. The control omits H first, then G, then F; its return adjustment changes only the currently omitted records. No real funds, market observations, causal estimates, confidence intervals, p-values or simulated samples are used. Group means are equal-weight arithmetic means across funds over one common year. Equal opening positions with no cash flows make the full-cohort mean equal to that original buy-and-hold basket’s simple return; the filtered mean uses a smaller denominator and is not the return earned by the original whole basket. Returns are assumed complete total-return inputs; no additional fee, tax, currency change, sales charge, new entry, merger, reinvestment after liquidation or missing-period return is modeled. An omitted record is never treated as a zero ending value. The directory is seen after the return period and does not supply an investable selection rule or a future return assumption.

The central idea

A performance average needs a defined membership rule as well as returns. Removing a record changes the reported denominator; it does not remove the investor’s original outcome.

01

Define the original group before reading its average

An end-of-year fund directory can look like a convenient starting point for comparing past performance. But a list of funds still present at the end of a period need not represent the whole group that existed at its beginning.

This article constructs a small original example with eight invented funds, labelled A through H. Each begins the same one-year period with CAD 10,000. Their assumed complete-period total returns, with all income retained and before fees and taxes, are +20%, +12%, +8%, +4%, 0%, −5%, −15% and −40%.

Every return remains known throughout the exercise. This is a fully specified teaching cohort, rather than a random sample, a market database or a forecast. The calculator does not infer missing returns or estimate a closure process.

The equal opening allocations total CAD 80,000. With no deposits, withdrawals or other adjustments, the simple return of that original basket equals the arithmetic mean of its eight individual one-year returns. This is a cross-sectional average over one common period, rather than an average of successive annual returns.

02

Change the directory without erasing the known outcomes

At the default setting, the end-of-year directory omits funds F, G and H. Their complete-year outcomes remain in the first chart, marked as omitted. The other five records are still listed.

This is an assumed reporting status at the end of the observation window. It does not assert that a poor return caused a closure, that a missing listing means liquidation, or that a discontinued fund necessarily lost all its value.

Carhart, Carpenter, Lynch and Musto’s working-paper abstract on mutual fund survivorship explains why the survival rule and the observation period matter when studying performance. The numerical cohort here is separate from that research and imports none of its empirical estimates.

The omission-count control removes H first, then G, then F from the reported directory. It leaves all eight original records available for the complete-cohort calculation. That distinction makes the selection visible instead of silently changing the historical population.

03

Calculate both means with their own denominators

The five listed returns add to 44 percentage points. Dividing by five gives a listed-group mean of 8.8%. The three omitted returns add to negative 60 percentage points, giving that group a mean of −20%.

All eight returns add to negative 16 percentage points. Dividing by eight gives a complete-cohort mean of −2%. The listed mean therefore exceeds the complete-cohort mean by 10.8 percentage points in this invented case.

The count chart explains why the denominator changes from eight to five. It is not a probability chart and does not estimate the chance that a fund will survive. There are exactly eight known members in the stated example.

Also keep percentage points separate from a relative percentage change. The difference between 8.8% and −2% is 10.8 percentage points. Describing it as a percentage increase over a negative baseline would obscure the comparison.

04

Weight the subgroup means by their original-cohort shares

The complete-cohort mean can be reconstructed from the two disjoint groups. The five listed funds represent five-eighths of the original cohort; the three omitted funds represent three-eighths.

The calculation is (5 ÷ 8) × 8.8% + (3 ÷ 8) × (−20%) = −2%. The waterfall displays a positive 5.5 percentage-point contribution from listed records and a negative 7.5 percentage-point contribution from omitted records.

Adding 8.8% directly to −20% would give the two groups equal weight despite their different membership counts. Their arithmetic sum is not the mean return of all eight funds.

This weighting works because the example uses equal opening amounts and one common complete year. An asset-weighted study would require its specified asset weights. A multi-period strategy with changing membership would need a return and rebalancing method for each period rather than this one-year identity.

05

An omitted record does not disappear from the investor’s original result

The listed positions finish with CAD 54,400: CAD 50,000 of opening allocations plus CAD 4,400 of gains. The omitted positions finish with CAD 24,000: CAD 30,000 initially, less CAD 6,000 of losses.

Together they finish with CAD 78,400, a CAD 1,600 decline on the original CAD 80,000. The 8.8% listed average does not turn that original basket into a gain. It summarizes a smaller group with only CAD 50,000 of opening capital.

Do not compare the two groups’ ending dollar totals as if both began with the same investment. Their capital and member counts differ. The metrics retain the original whole-basket ending value so the reporting filter cannot erase its losses.

An actual liquidation, merger or distribution would require its real cash and successor records. This example assigns an end-year directory status after a complete known year; it does not fabricate an unobserved post-closure return or assume that missing history is worth zero.

06

The sign of the gap depends on the outcomes omitted

The sensitivity control adds an assumed percentage-point adjustment only to the records currently omitted. It holds the listed records and directory membership fixed. This changes the invented underlying outcomes rather than estimating a statistical correction.

With three omissions and a +60 percentage-point adjustment, their returns become +55%, +45% and +20%. The complete-cohort mean becomes 20.5%, while the listed mean remains 8.8%. The listed-minus-complete gap is now negative 11.7 percentage points.

The sign has reversed because the omitted group is now stronger. A label such as missing, closed or discontinued does not by itself establish the omitted performance. The data and selection mechanism need examination.

With no omissions, all eight records are still listed and both means equal one another. The adjustment has no recipients, so it changes nothing. No omitted-group mean is defined when that group has zero members; its contribution to the full-cohort mean is simply zero.

07

Ask how the history was assembled before using it in a plan

Investor.gov’s performance-claims bulletin discusses calculation methods, excluded costs and selective presentation. These are useful questions alongside the membership rule: what period, which records, what return definition and which expenses?

For a real database, check how it handles new entries, name changes, mergers, liquidations, incomplete periods and records removed after the fact. Retaining a list of discontinued names is not enough if their relevant return histories are absent or incompatible.

This article supplies no evidence of manager skill, market-wide bias or a future expected return. Its eight funds are invented, and the directory is observed after the modeled year. Selecting only those records retrospectively is not an investment rule a reader could necessarily have followed at the beginning.

A financial plan still needs defensible return assumptions, uncertainty, fees, taxes and a workable cash calendar. Use this example to inspect the history behind an average before allowing that number to drive a savings target or retirement projection.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Four original hypothetical figures describe a fully observed eight-fund cohort over one common year. Directory omissions are assumed statuses, rather than real fund closures or estimated survival probabilities. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
